A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MR3 research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison and matching across renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original multilingual benchmark experiments, language-strategy comparisons, automated reasoning assessments, and human rubric ratings.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds policy-alignment results, training ablations, and expanded human evaluations.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 adds a downstream procedure using MR3 for DPO post-training of Qwen3-30B-A3B. This extends the workflow, while MR3's dataset construction, filtering, SFT objective, and language-forcing procedure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds policy-alignment training using Aya, m-RewardBench, and PolyMath, and evaluates generated responses on m-ArenaHard-v2.0, MCLM, and INCLUDE. This extends coverage beyond reward-model judgments. Human assessment expands from English/Chinese rubrics to a study across 12 languages; the original reward benchmarks and 72-language training corpus remain.

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 add DeepSeek-R1-14B and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct comparisons while retaining the earlier reward baselines. New comparisons include Nemotron-based DPO alignment in Table 4 and GRPO-based RLVR against SFT in Table 28, substantially broadening the comparative evidence.

E3.justification: New protocols cover additional backbones, DPO evaluation with GPT-4.1-mini and fixed reference position, and a 50K SFT plus 50K RLVR comparison against 100K SFT. The earlier GPT-5-mini reasoning assessment sampled only correct outputs; v2's human assessment includes correct and incorrect outputs, with 15 questions per annotator.

E4.justification: Appendices G–I add data-size and teacher-strength ablations, quantitative curriculum comparisons, SFT-versus-RLVR analysis, unseen-language subgroup analysis, and human reasoning case studies. The earlier language/translation comparisons remain, while the automated reasoning-quality assessment is removed. Table 27 explicitly reproduces prior R3 ablations rather than reporting newly performed MR3 experiments.

E5.justification: v2 first reports five-run means and standard deviations in the main benchmark tables, five-seed information for ablations, and 95% confidence intervals for DPO win rates. v1 reported variability for rubric and reasoning ratings but did not specify equivalent repeated-run reporting for its main benchmarks.

E6.justification: Main-table estimates change: MR3-Qwen3-14B's RewardBench entry becomes 90.79 ± 0.25 instead of 91.12. New alignment, ablation, and human results substantially expand the findings. Table 4 reports overall m-ArenaHard win rates of 39.1% before alignment, 45.2% with MR3-based DPO, and 47.0% with Nemotron-based DPO. The legacy detailed benchmark tables retain their numerical values.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5, the SFT loss, and Appendix C.1's task definitions are unchanged. The additional experiments introduce no substantive formal derivations, theoretical assumptions, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add contributions concerning downstream preference optimization and human-validated reasoning and rubrics, explicitly including languages unseen during MR3 training. The original claims about broad language coverage and competitive, compact reward models remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking teacher quality and SFT supervision to rubric adherence, and suggests that weaker target-language benchmark performance may partly reflect evaluation bias despite favorable human ratings. Human feedback and case studies introduce specific translation, code-switching, and reasoning failures. The original limitations section is largely unchanged.

D1.justification: New disclosures include alignment-data composition and deduplication, annotation instructions and sampling, GRPO rewards, and SFT/RLVR hardware and training-time comparisons. Core SFT/inference settings and the access link remain. However, v1's identification of the Qwen-235B translation model disappears even though translated-reasoning comparisons are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting DPO, additional models and benchmarks, position bias, and ensemble metrics. Related work now explicitly identifies R3 as the underlying rubric-based framework extended to multilingual settings. The broader literature organization and positioning remain similar.

P1.justification: Rewriting is concentrated in the abstract, contributions, curriculum description, baseline presentation, and language-strategy discussion. Alignment, human-evaluation, and ablation subsections are inserted, with terminology and header updates. The six-section main outline and most existing method and prompt text remain intact.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are restyled or redrawn, including revised colors, legends, and caption placement. Main tables gain model rows and uncertainty displays, and Table 2 loses its average column. New alignment, subgroup, ablation, human-evaluation, and case-study tables substantially expand the displays; earlier detailed Tables 7–20 become Tables 9–22.

improvement.justification: v1 assessed reasoning automatically only on correct outputs and supplied little quantitative support for several training choices. v2 adds human assessment including failures, substantive training ablations, downstream alignment tests, and repeated-run uncertainty, substantially strengthening the empirical support. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including small human samples, removal of the translator identification, and apparently swapped MM-Eval/IndoPref headings in new ablation tables. The DPO results support downstream usefulness without establishing superiority over Nemotron on every benchmark.
